academicPassage.title: When Sleep Helps—and When It Doesn’t
academicPassage.passage:
Popular articles often claim that sleeping after studying ‘locks in’ learning, but the research is more conditional. Many experiments show that performance improves after sleep compared with an equal period awake, suggesting a role for consolidation. Yet the size of the benefit depends on what happens before and after sleep.

One major factor is interference. If participants learn new, similar material soon after training, the original memory trace can be weakened. Sleep may protect memories partly by reducing exposure to competing information. Accordingly, studies that control participants’ post-learning activities often find stronger effects than studies conducted in realistic settings where people continue to work, socialize, and use digital media.

Another factor is sleep architecture. Fragmented sleep can reduce slow-wave activity, which is associated with stabilizing certain kinds of declarative memories. Short naps sometimes help, but only when they contain sufficient slow-wave sleep. Finally, individual differences matter: stress, chronotype, and prior sleep debt can all influence outcomes.

Taken together, the evidence supports a genuine contribution of sleep to memory, while also explaining why some individuals experience little improvement. Rather than promising guaranteed gains, scientists increasingly emphasize designing schedules that minimize interference and support consistent sleep quality.

It says benefits exist but are conditional on interference, sleep architecture, and individual differences.

academicPassage.title: Why Storage Planning Is a Matching Problem
academicPassage.passage:
Energy storage is often discussed as a single solution for renewable integration, but the grid uses storage for multiple functions. Short-duration systems can respond within seconds, stabilizing frequency and smoothing brief ramps in solar output. Longer-duration systems, in contrast, address sustained mismatches between supply and demand, such as evening peaks or extended periods of low wind.

Because these functions differ, the ‘best’ technology depends on local constraints. Lithium-ion batteries are well suited to fast response, yet repeated deep cycling and high temperatures accelerate degradation. Flow batteries can provide long duration with less cycle-related wear, but they require more space and careful handling of electrolytes. Pumped hydro offers large capacity and long lifetimes, but it is geographically limited and can take years to permit.

Planning therefore involves trade-offs rather than universal rankings. Engineers evaluate not only cost per kilowatt-hour stored, but also reliability benefits and ancillary services. A portfolio that mixes technologies can reduce risk, especially when future demand patterns and supply chains are uncertain. In this sense, storage planning resembles insurance: decision-makers pay for flexibility today to avoid expensive failures tomorrow.

Why (C) is wrong: It says storage has multiple functions.
